statement: Holiday-park lodge hot tubs tested by hand at every changeover — HSG282 logs patchy and Legionella risk — Holiday parks and glamping sites with dozens to hundreds of lodge hot tubs must control Legionella under HSE's HSG282, which covers domestic-type hot tubs used in a business such as holiday-park rentals: frequent disinfectant/pH checks and records. Staff test by hand between guests and logs are patchy. Hot-tub-linked outbreaks lead to closures, enforcement and compensation claims; manual testing takes ~10–20 minutes per tub per day.
buyer_job_title: Holiday Park Operations / Maintenance Manager (multi-lodge operators)

statement: Thousands of Type 3 TMVs serviced on fixed cycles because nobody can prove they're still mixing correctly — HTM 04-01 requires Type 3 thermostatic mixing valves in healthcare, with in-service testing and servicing (D08 schedule); hospitals pay water-hygiene contractors per valve per visit across thousands of outlets, yet failing TMVs still deliver scalding water (scalding was historically an NHS 'Never Event') or run cold enough to grow Legionella.
buyer_job_title: Water Safety Responsible Person / Head of Estates Compliance

statement: Liquid nitrogen storage dewar boils down between weekly top-ups — cryopreserved cell lines and vials lost — Standalone LN2 dewars in core facilities and biobanks lose nitrogen daily; if a weekly top-up is missed, a lid is left ajar or the vacuum jacket degrades (boil-off rises), vapour-phase temperature climbs and years of cell lines/vials are lost (~£5k–£100k+ to rebuild a cell bank or re-collect samples). Checks are a weekly dipstick reading on a paper log; vacuum failure goes unnoticed until the dewar is empty.

Hired breakers and grinders used without real trigger-time records — HAVS prosecutions with £100k+ fines — Employers must assess and control hand-arm vibration exposure under the Control of Vibration at Work Regulations 2005, and HSE regularly prosecutes (Stonewater £140k, a car dealership £200k+, Places for People £600k). Most vibrating tools on sites are hired, and hirers rely on paper estimates of trigger time; dedicated HAV monitoring systems are expensive and don't move with hired tools.
buyer_job_title: Contractor Health & Safety Manager, sold as a hire-desk add-on by the hire company

statement: Executors of empty probate homes can't prove the insurer's inspection and drain-down conditions — A deceased person's home sits empty for 6–18 months during probate. Unoccupied-home insurers require weekly/fortnightly inspections and water off/drained (or heating at a minimum temperature) in winter. Executors and solicitors live far away, so a burst pipe claim (~£10–30k+) is declined and the estate or solicitor bears it.
buyer_job_title: Private Client/Probate Partner at a solicitors' firm or a professional estate administrator

statement: Culvert trash screens block in a storm and flood homes; councils still drive round to look — Debris blinds council-owned culvert trash screens during storms, backing water into homes and roads; Southend spent ~£15k and four days clearing one culvert blockage. Councils run weekly plus post-rainfall inspection rounds; existing telemetry is costly (Fife quoted ~£3.4k install + ~£1.3k/yr for one screen; Carmarthenshire ~£40k for a network) so most screens remain unmonitored.
buyer_job_title: Flood Risk / Land Drainage Manager at the Lead Local Flood Authority
sector: Local councils – parks, highways, street assets

statement: Church roof alarms rely on phone-line diallers the PSTN switch-off breaks, putting lead-theft cover at risk — The main church insurer limits metal-theft cover unless an approved, monitored roof alarm is fitted. Existing alarms cost ~£3k-£5k plus maintenance, and many use landline diallers that fail with the digital switchover. A lead theft costs from ~£10k to ~£400k per church.
buyer_job_title: Churchwarden / PCC (with Diocesan Advisory Committee approval), reached via insurer-approved installers
sector: Places of worship, community halls & charities

statement: Warehouse sprinkler pump-house weekly test log faked or skipped, so the insurer challenges the claim — LPC Rules/TB203 and BS EN 12845 require a weekly sprinkler pump start test (diesel run ≥30 min), fuel/oil checks and valve-pressure readings, all logged. On lightly staffed DCs the weekly test is skipped, frost hits the pump house, or the diesel battery is flat. An impaired system found after a fire puts a £m warehouse loss and insurer conditions precedent in play.
buyer_job_title: Site Facilities Manager or Property Manager of a distribution centre

statement: HMO weekly fire alarm tests skipped or unrecorded: civil penalties up to £30k per offence — HMO managers must keep fire alarms working under the HMO Management Regulations 2006 and councils expect weekly tests and records (LACORS/BS 5839-6); councils issue civil penalties up to £30k per offence and fines (e.g. Gateshead ~£42k including missing checks/records, Liverpool ~£20k). Agents either drive to each HMO weekly or rely on tenants, and panel fault LEDs go unnoticed.

Little-used pool and spa changing-room showers — weekly Legionella flushing and monthly temperature checks done by hand — Leisure centres and spas have dozens of showers and TMVs. ACoP L8 / HSG274 requires little-used outlets to be flushed weekly and sentinel temperatures to be checked monthly, so duty staff walk round flushing and water-hygiene contractors charge per outlet to take temperatures. Records are often incomplete, which is a recurring theme in HSE Legionella enforcement.
buyer_job_title: Leisure Trust Compliance / Facilities Manager (Legionella responsible person)

statement: Small frozen-food and ice-cream distributors lack the transport temperature records quick-frozen food law requires — Quick-frozen food rules require transport to have temperature recording instruments and records kept (~1 year). Small ice-cream and frozen wholesale distributors running converted vans rely on cab displays and paper sheets, which leads to customer audit and EHO findings. A fridge-unit failure mid-round can write off a van load (~£3k-£10k) with no evidence of when it started.
buyer_job_title: Owner / Transport Manager of an independent frozen-food or ice-cream wholesale distributor

statement: Floor-stored grain heats in hot spots between weekly spear probes; loads rejected for insects or mycotoxins — Red Tractor assessors expect records of crop temperature and moisture monitoring in store (weekly after harvest). Manual probing misses hot spots, and heating grain leads to insect infestation, downgrades or rejection (~£2k-£10k per load or heap) and claims from merchants.
buyer_job_title: Farm Manager / Arable Business Owner; on-farm co-op store manager

statement: Emergency safety showers and eyewashes: unproven weekly flush, unseen real activations — Chemical-handling plants should flush emergency showers and eyewashes weekly (ANSI Z358.1 in the US; BS EN 15154 and L8 dead-leg Legionella advice in the UK). Flushes are missed, so stagnant water reaches an injured eye. A real activation in a remote corner at night goes unseen while a splashed worker is alone. OSHA serious citations run ~$16k each (US), and UK RIDDOR investigations follow.
buyer_job_title: EHS Manager at a chemical, plating or water-treatment-chemicals plant

statement: Void council homes: insurer demands 7-day inspections and drain-down proof or the escape-of-water claim is refused — Insurer unoccupancy conditions typically require internal and external inspections at least every 7 days, water drained or heating held at ~5-10°C, and logs kept 12 months; breach voids escape-of-water and malicious damage cover. Social landlords with hundreds of voids pay security firms for screens and weekly inspections, and still get burst pipes and break-ins.
buyer_job_title: Voids Manager / Asset Manager at housing association or council

statement: Independent forecourts reconcile wetstock by hand — slow leaks, theft and short deliveries surface weeks late — Petroleum licensing conditions and Environment Agency guidance expect wetstock records and leak detection proportionate to risk, and trade sources say reconciliation must be daily. Many independent dealers still reconcile from dips or by reading the tank-gauge console by hand, so leaks, theft and short deliveries surface weeks later. Clean-up can cost £100k+, trade press cites EA fines of up to ~£20k, and a 0.5% loss on 2m litres a year is ~£14k.
